stories.body: Israelis are voting in their first general election since the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack and the regional wars that followed. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, seeking to extend his rule at the head of a far-right alliance, is in a close contest with centrist rival Gadi Eisenkot and faces questions over security failures, his corruption trial, ultra-Orthodox military service and the exclusion of Arab-led parties. The outcome could shape Israel's approach to Gaza, the West Bank and Iran, while also carrying implications for the United States ahead of its congressional elections.
stories.headline: Israel votes in its first election since the October 7 attack, with Netanyahu facing a pivotal test

stories.body: Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agreed to continue talks on regional peace and security after senior officials met in Tehran. Saudi Arabia said the visit was intended to open channels to prevent renewed military escalation, while Pakistani officials said discussions included a proposed regional non-aggression arrangement, US-Iran negotiations, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the Strait of Hormuz and the US blockade of Iranian ports. The talks came as Saudi-led forces reported intercepting further Houthi missiles and drones aimed at the kingdom.
stories.headline: Regional powers hold talks with Iran to avert renewed Middle East conflict

stories.body: Jordan said it carried out airstrikes on armed groups in southern Syria in response to Friday's attack on a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, which killed nine people and wounded dozens. Jordan said the operation killed or injured militants and destroyed vehicles, but Syrian authorities said at least seven civilians, including three children and a woman, were killed in strikes on sites in Daraa and Suweyda. Jordan said the operation was coordinated with Damascus; Syria denied that account, launched an investigation and closed the Nassib border crossing.
stories.headline: Jordan strikes targets in Syria in retaliation for a church attack

stories.body: A UN independent commission of inquiry said Israeli authorities and forces had committed crimes against humanity in the occupied West Bank, including extermination, torture, rape and other sexual violence, and were continuing to commit genocidal acts in Gaza despite a ceasefire. The commission said military operations, settler violence, killings and destruction formed part of a widespread and systematic attack on Palestinian civilians. Israel rejected the report as a misinformation campaign and called for the commission's dissolution; the body does not speak for the UN as a whole.
stories.headline: UN panel accuses Israel of crimes against humanity in the West Bank and genocide in Gaza

stories.body: China's stock market has lost an estimated $2.4 trillion since May as investors question whether the country's AI boom can produce sustainable profits amid weak domestic demand and the threat of further Western technology restrictions. The Shanghai STAR 50 technology index has fallen 40% since June, while major indexes have declined by about 20%. Beijing has invested heavily in AI and robotics, but many companies face thin margins, limited consumer demand and uncertainty over US restrictions on Chinese technology and components.
stories.headline: Chinese markets lose trillions as the US-China AI race weighs on investors

stories.body: Anthropic's public filing for a planned Nasdaq listing reported $16.3 billion in revenue and more than $80.7 billion in net losses for the first half of 2026. The Claude developer said advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks if they are misused, replicated, weaponized or allowed substantial autonomy without adequate safeguards. The company has not disclosed the timing, share count or price range for its offering, which is expected to be a major test of investor appetite for a fully AI-focused public company.
stories.headline: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals soaring revenue, deep losses and warnings of catastrophic AI risk

stories.body: French student representatives said they would continue mobilizing after meeting Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, despite government promises to reform the university-admissions system known as Parcoursup. Students demanding more investment in schools, more teachers and broader education reforms called the proposed changes insufficient, noting that a replacement system is not planned until 2028 and could depend on the next government. The demonstrations, which began in September, have expanded into a broader movement and at times turned violent.
stories.headline: French student leaders call for continued protests despite government concessions

stories.body: Federal prosecutors have moved to charge former FBI director James Comey with two counts involving the alleged disclosure of national-defense information to the New York Times in 2016. The charges were filed through a criminal information rather than a grand-jury indictment, and Comey denies wrongdoing, calling the case an abusive campaign of political retribution. His lawyer said two previous teams of prosecutors had investigated the alleged disclosure and declined to bring charges; legal observers also questioned whether the case falls outside the statute of limitations.
stories.headline: Former FBI director James Comey faces a third set of federal charges under Trump

stories.body: President Donald Trump said he would offer a $1 million reward for information that leads to a voter-fraud conviction before the November 3 midterm elections. He provided no details about how the reward would be funded or administered. The pledge follows his repeated false claims that he won the 2020 presidential election.
stories.headline: Trump offers a $1 million reward for tips leading to voter-fraud convictions before the midterms

stories.body: Researchers and community groups warn that AI chatbots can give non-English-speaking voters inaccurate, incomplete or confusing election information, potentially creating another barrier ahead of the midterms. A September study by the Institute for Strategic Dialogue found chatbot accuracy fell 16% for Spanish-language voter-information prompts, with answers more likely to omit relevant details or use overly literal translations. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google said they are working to improve non-English support and election-information safeguards, while some civic groups are building their own language-specific tools or avoiding AI for in-language outreach.
stories.headline: AI chatbots give less reliable election information to non-English-speaking voters, researchers warn

stories.body: Several Republican incumbents who are retiring or were defeated by Trump-backed candidates are declining to campaign for their potential successors, exposing tensions within the party ahead of the midterms. Texas Senator John Cornyn has raised money for other Republicans but not for Attorney General Ken Paxton, who beat him in the primary; North Carolina Senator Thom Tillis has remained distant from Michael Whatley's Senate campaign; and Nevada Representative Mark Amodei says he will not vote for his party's nominee. Trump-aligned groups argue that such defections help Democrats, while the incumbents cite concerns about candidates' records and the party's direction.
stories.headline: Trump-spurned Republican incumbents withhold support from the party’s nominees

stories.body: Spain's government has softened a proposed decree governing large data centers after industry criticism and a critical report from the competition regulator. The rules would now apply to facilities of at least 10 megawatts rather than 1 megawatt, and would give operators more time and flexibility to meet renewable-energy requirements, including through batteries and shorter power-purchase agreements. Large centers would still ultimately need to demonstrate that 80% of their electricity consumption is covered by associated renewable generation, while a five-year transitional system would impose less stringent targets in exchange for allowing the grid operator to curtail their power in emergencies.
stories.headline: Spain relaxes environmental requirements for new data centers

stories.body: Spain has begun involuntarily returning migrants who arrived during the mass entry into Ceuta to Morocco after their applications for international protection were denied. Interior Ministry sources said 16 people, most of them from sub-Saharan Africa, were returned on Friday after they did not appeal the decisions within the allotted period. The returns differ from voluntary returns that had been taking place in Ceuta in recent weeks.
stories.headline: Spain begins returning Ceuta migrants to Morocco after denying their asylum claims

stories.body: At least 19 people were arrested in Bilbao after unrest surrounding a canceled appearance by far-right content creator Vito Quiles. Following a protest outside the University of Deusto, groups set fire to vehicles and rubbish containers, damaged street furniture, attacked shops and threw stones at police and a police station, according to the Basque police. Quiles said he canceled the event for security reasons, while Basque leaders condemned the violence and said authorities were investigating those responsible.
stories.headline: Violent unrest spreads to Bilbao, with at least 19 arrests reported

stories.body: Judges have ordered closed detention for three minors arrested in Saturday's unrest in central Barcelona, while other minors received precautionary measures including supervised release and bans on attending demonstrations or gatherings. Fifty-one adults appeared before a court and were released under conditions. Police reported 130 arrests, including 76 minors, although prosecutors cited 89 minors; the cases involve alleged public disorder, damage, burglary and assault on officers.
stories.headline: Three minors are placed in closed detention after Barcelona’s weekend unrest

stories.body: Catalonia's Interior Ministry said the Mossos d'Esquadra will seek urgent judicial authorization to identify administrators of TikTok and messaging accounts used to call young people to Saturday's unrest in Barcelona. Authorities want platforms to close groups that encourage violence, looting and public disorder; a main Telegram group with about 1,900 users was shut down for violating the platform's terms. Police are investigating the organizers and the spread of calls associated with the Blocus platform, which circulated rapidly among students through social-media and messaging groups.
stories.headline: Barcelona moves to identify and shut messaging groups used to promote the unrest

stories.body: The widow and children of a former Barcelona Metro worker who died from mesothelioma are seeking €239,401 from Ferrocarril Metropolità de Barcelona, part of TMB, alleging failures in workplace safety protections. Courts previously recognized that the worker's cancer and 2019 death resulted from occupational asbestos exposure during his work on electrical installations and signaling from 1988 to 2008. A hearing beginning Wednesday will consider whether the company took the legally required measures to protect staff and is liable for damages; TMB said it does not comment on ongoing court cases.
stories.headline: Family of Barcelona Metro worker who died after asbestos exposure seeks €239,000 from TMB
